Apple's commercial secrets lawsuit against OpenAI has been reassigned to US District Judge Edward Davila, replacing the magistrate judge who was originally assigned to handle the case. Details as follows.

New judge takes over, October hearing cancelled

When a civil lawsuit is filed in the Northern District of California, the case is randomly assigned to a federal district judge or a magistrate judge. If assigned to a magistrate judge, all parties must state whether they consent to the judge hearing the entire case.

This is because federal district judges have the authority to oversee federal civil cases from start to finish, while magistrate judges can only do so with the consent of all parties.

On the day Apple filed its trade secrets lawsuit against two former employees, OpenAI, and io Products, the company founded by Jony Ive, the case was randomly assigned to Magistrate Judge Virginia K. DeMarchi.

This means all parties involved in the lawsuit must submit a form indicating whether they consent to Judge DeMarchi trying the entire case.

Apple appears to have rejected this arrangement. The company filed a consent or refusal declaration yesterday (the document has not yet been made public), which appears to have triggered the procedure for reassigning the case to a federal district judge.

There do not appear to be any other documents explaining the reassignment, which strongly suggests Apple ticked the box on the form refusing magistrate jurisdiction.

As a result, the case has been reassigned to US District Judge Edward Davila, while Magistrate Judge Nathanael Cousins handles matters relating to discovery.

With the reassignment of the case, the initial case management conference originally scheduled for October 13 before Judge DeMarchi has been cancelled and will need to be rescheduled before Judge Davila.

However, two other sets of deadlines remain in effect: the parties must discuss settlement proposals and discovery plans by September 22, and submit initial disclosure documents and a joint case management statement by October 6.
